Work and Power
Whenever a force moves something, work is done. It is a measure of
the amount of energy used in moving the object. Work is measured in
joules (J). If a force acts but nothing moves then no work is done.
Work can be calculated using the following equation:
    Work done = force applied x distance moved                   or     W =
F x d
where W is the work done (J), F is the force applied (N) and d is the
distance moved (m).

Power is the rate at which work is done, or how fast energy is used.
Power is measured in Watts (W), work in Joules (J) and time measured in
seconds (s).

Work
Work done is defined as product of the force and the distance over which the force is applied.

Work is done when a force is applied to an object and the object is moved
through a distance.

For example, when you lift a load you are applying a force over a distance so
you are doing work.

When you push a shopping trolley around a supermarket you are applying a
force over a distance, therefore you are doing work.

When a car is moving on a motorway, a force is being applied over a distance
and work is being done.

Work done: = force x distance
W=Fxs

       W is measures in joules.
       F is measure in newtons.
       s is measured in metres.
       When work is done, energy is transferred.

Example questions:
Question 1
A fork lift moves 34m carrying a 1023N box across the warehouse floor. How
much work is done by the fork lift?

Answer:
W=Fxs
W = 1023N x 34m
W = 34,782 J                  The forklift does 34,782J of work.

Question 2
A crane operator on a building site slowly
raises a loaded crate of mass 1500 kg at a
steady speed.

a) What is the weight W of the crate?

b) What is the upwards pull P on the crate?

c) How much work is done by P in raising the crate to a height of 4 m?

d) What is the gain in gravitational potential energy of the crate when it is at a
height of 4 m.

e) What is the gravitational potential energy of the crate when it is a height of 9
m?
 Answer
a) The gravitational pull acting on a mass of 1 kg is 9.8 N.
So the gravitational pull on a mass of 1500 kg is 1500 x 9.8 = 14 700 N
Weight of loaded crate = 14 700 N
b) Upwards pull P = weight of crate = 14 700 N
c) Work done by P in raising crate to a height of 4 m
= force applied to crate x distance moved
= 15 000 x 4
= 60 000 J
d) Work done by P in raising crate to a height of 4 m
= gain in gravitational potential energy
So, gain in gravitational potential energy = 60 000 J
e) Gravitational potential energy, Ep= mgh
= 1500 x10 x 9
= 135 000 J
Gravitational potential energy of the crate at a height of 9 m = 135 000 J

Practice Problems:
1. Calculate the amount of work done when moving a 567N crate a distance of
20 meters.

2. A fallen tree of mass 700kg lifted 2.75 meters. How much work is done?

Getting oxygen into your body is vital for our survival. Many different diseases of the
lungs and respiratory system prevent you from being able to breathe as deeply as
normal and breathing may cause you to cough or wheeze. Common diseases of the
lungs include asthma, emphysema, bronchitis and pneumonia. These diseases may
be chronic, which means they are long lasting or occur over and over again. Other
diseases are acute, which means they come on rapidly and last a short time.


Asthma
Asthma is a chronic disease in which the bronchi in the lungs are swollen and tender.
In this condition the bronchi react to factors in the environment, known as triggers.
Triggers such as tobacco smoke, dust and pollens cause muscles in the walls of the
bronchi to contract, making the airways narrow, as shown in Figure 3.1.1. The cell
lining of the bronchi produces extra mucus. The mucus reduces the space inside the
bronchi even more and the person has difficulty breathing.

When people with asthma feel an attack coming on, they use puffers. The puffer
contains chemicals that relax the muscles of the bronchi. This allows the bronchi to
open up and the person is able to breathe freely again.




      Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Figure 3.1.1
The passage through which air can pass is very narrow during an asthma attack.


Emphysema
Emphysema is a chronic lung disease in which the bronchi, alveoli and blood
capillaries are damaged. Emphysema is usually caused by smoking or long-term
exposure to air pollutants (chemicals) and dust.

The tissues of healthy bronchi and alveoli are elastic, which means that they are able
to stretch and then return to their original shape. When bronchi and alveoli are
exposed to pollutants and dust over long periods of time, they lose their ability to
stretch. The bronchi become narrow and the alveoli break. Damage to the alveoli
creates larger spaces within the lungs. Having large spaces reduces the surface area
for gas exchange. The blood capillaries surrounding the alveoli are also damaged
and less carbon dioxide and oxygen can be carried to the alveoli and away from
them.

Compare the photograph of the alveoli of a person with emphysema in Figure 3.1.2
with the alveoli of a healthy person shown in Figure 3.1.3.




        Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Figure 3.1.2
Alveoli of someone who is suffering from emphysema




Figure 3.1.3
Alveoli of a healthy person.

People with emphysema become breathless during physical activity and frequently
have chest infections. They often have a bluish colour to their skin, especially around
their lips. This bluish colour is known as cyanosis and is caused by a lack of oxygen
in their blood.

Emphysema develops slowly. Damaged alveoli and tissues of the bronchi do not
repair themselves so the damage is permanent. A person with advanced
emphysema has to breathe hard in an attempt to exhale fully and to get enough air
into their lungs. Open your mouth as wide as it can go and then try blowing out a
candle or match without making an ‘O’ shape with your lips. It is difficult. This is what
breathing is like for people with emphysema, all the time.

The heart pumps blood around the body in the circulatory system. In the circulatory
system are three types of blood vessels. They each have a different structure that is
related to their function.


Arteries
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. In the arteries, the blood is under high
pressure from the heart beat. As seen in Figure 3.2.1, the walls of the arteries are
strong, thick and elastic to withstand the pressure. Large arteries branch into smaller
and smaller arteries, which spread and carry blood to all parts of the body. Eventually
the branches of the arteries become very fine, and are known as capillaries.




       Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Figure 3.2.1
Structure of a an artery


Capillaries
Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels. Capillaries are so small that red blood
cells can only just squeeze through them. The walls are similar to the innermost layer
of the arteries, as seen in Figure 3.2.2.




Figure 3.2.2
Structure of a capillary

The flow of blood in the capillaries is fairly slow (about 1 mm per second) and by this
stage the blood is not under pressure. The capillaries reach nearly every cell of the
body. The capillaries then join together forming larger vessels called veins.

       Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2356 2
 Veins
Veins carry blood back towards the heart. The blood is no longer under pressure and
it is moving against gravity. The structure of a vein can be seen in Figure 3.2.3.




Figure 3.2.3
Structure of a vein

                                       5: Natural selection

This worksheet uses some invented data to test your understanding of the principles of
natural selection. It also deals with some aspects of ecology.

A farmer's grain crop is under attack from an insect pest. This pest, the corn weevil, bores
holes in the seeds of the crop in summer and lays its eggs. The adults then die. The eggs
hatch into larvae, which feed from the seeds until they mature and are ready to fly off. The
adult weevils feed from a different food plant. They mate and then hibernate through the
winter, starting the cycle again the next year. For every adult weevil, an average of 5 offspring
are produced every year.

The farmer has tried to control the corn weevil by spraying his crops in summer with an
insecticide called 'Bugloss'. When he first used this, it was very successful. Only 15% of the
immature weevils survived the application of Bugloss. However, in the last year of spraying,
25% survived. The corn weevil is known to develop a mutation which makes it resistant to
Bugloss, and the farmer has been advised that resistance has developed in the pest attacking
his crop. This resistance is inherited.

non-resistant weevils produce 5 offspring per year, answer the following questions:

LONGMAN GCSE BIOLOGY WORKSHEETS

                                        6: Mendel's peas

This worksheet tests your understanding of Mendel's breeding experiments and looks his
results in light of the discovery of genes.

Gregor Mendel published the results of his experiments on the genetics of the garden pea
plant in 1865. He carried out a number of experiments on contrasting pairs of phenotypic
characteristics, such as green or yellow pod colour. For example, when he crossed plants that
were pure-breeding for green pods with plants that were pure-breeding for yellow pods, he
found that all the offspring (called the F1 generation) had green pods. However, when he
crossed-fertilised these F1 plants, the next generation (called the F2) consisted of some plants
that had green, and others yellow, pods. He found similar results for several other contrasting
pairs of characteristics.

The F2 offspring for the pod colour experiment and six other experiments on different
contrasting characters is shown in the table:

Characters of 'parent' plants         F1 generation       Numbers in F2 generation           Ratio of
                                                                                             numbers in
                                                                                             F2
green pod × yellow pod                all green        428 green : 152 yellow                2.82 : 1
inflated pod × constricted pod*       all inflated     882 inflated : 299 constricted        2.95 : 1
round peas × wrinkled peas            all round        5474 round : 1850 wrinkled
yellow peas × green peas              all yellow       6022 yellow : 2001 green
long stem × short stem                all long         787 long : 277 short
purple flower × white flower          all purple       705 purple : 224 white
flower along stem × flower at tip     all along stem   651 along stem : 207 at tip
* Inflated pods look fat – constricted pods have the peas visible in them.
Questions

1. Why could Mendel not have used the word 'genetics'?

2. What do we mean by the word 'phenotype', as in 'phenotypic characters'?

3. Calculate the missing ratios of numbers in the F2 generation to complete the last column of
the table.

4. Using the symbol 'R' for the allele for round peas and 'r' for the allele for wrinkled, draw
genetic diagrams to explain the results of the cross between plants with round and wrinkled
peas, for both the F1 and F2 results. Use these words in the correct places on your diagram
homozygous, heterozygous, dominant, recessive and genotype.

5. What word would we now use to describe the genetics of the 'pure-breeding' parents?

6. Your answer to question 4 should predict that the phenotypes of the F2 generation are in
the ratio 3 : 1. The ratios in the table are very close to, but not exactly equal to, 3 : 1. There
are a number of reasons for this difference. Suggest three.

When Mendel published his findings in 1865, no one knew about the existence of
chromosomes, so Mendel could not explain his findings in terms of structures in the cell. In
the light of this handicap, his work was an outstanding achievement, because it led him to
propose that

    §   'Particles of inheritance' (which we now called genes) exist
    §   Particles are present in pairs in 'body' cells




Longman GCSE Biology                     ©Pearson Education 2002                               Page 1 of 2
     §   Pairs of particles separate during the formation of gametes, so that each gamete only
        carries one of each pair
    §   Particles can have dominant and recessive forms (alleles).

Nowadays we know about chromosomes and meiosis, so we can explain what is happening
inside the cell to produce Mendel's results.

7. By referring your genetic diagrams for crosses between round and wrinkled peas (question
4), draw a series of simple diagrams of cells (containing just one pair of chromosomes for
simplicity) to show what happens to the alleles for round and wrinkled phenotypes during
formation of gametes (meiosis) and then during fertilisation.

Writing Equations

Chemists write equations to represent what is happening in a chemical reaction. Equations are
useful because they provide an easy way to show complex reactions.

Word Equations

    The simplest form of chemical equation is a word equation.
    The most general word equation is:
       Reactants → products
    This general equation can then be expanded to:
       Substance A + Substance B → Substance C + Substance D
    For example, consider the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid. This reaction
     produces magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas. It can be written as a word equation.
       Reactants → products
       Magnesium + Hydrochloric acid → Magnesium chloride + Hydrogen gas

Example 1: Lead reacts with oxygen gas to produce lead (IV) oxide. Write a word equation to
describe the reaction.




Using Formulae

    A chemical equation tells you even more information if it includes the element symbols and
     chemical formulae of all the substances involved.
    In the example above, the reactants and products can be written using symbols for the
     elements and compounds.
    The reaction can be written as:
       Mg + HCl →MgCl2 + H2

Rules for Formula Equations
    Metals are written as single atoms: copper is written as Cu and iron is written as Fe
    Non-metal gases are written as diatomic molecules: oxygen is written as O 2, hydrogen is
     written as H2, chlorine is written as Cl2 etc.

Writing Ionic Formulae
An ionic solid is formed when positive ion and negative ion react to form
a compound. The positive ion and negative ion are attracted to each
other because they have opposite charges.

                     Rules for Writing Ionic Formulae

  1. Only positive and negative ions will combine.
     A positive sodium ion, Na+ will combine with a negative chloride
     ion, Cl-.
     A positive sodium ion, Na+ will not combine with a positive calcium
     ion, Ca2+.

  2. The overall charge of the formula is neutral.
     The formula for sodium chloride is NaCl. The positive charge on the
     sodium ion is balanced by the negative charge on the chloride ion
     so the formula is neutral.

  3. The number of each ion is written on the lower right hand
     side of the ion.
     The formula for calcium chloride is CaCl2. This shows that for each
     calcium ion, there are two chloride ions.

  4. Where only one ion is needed, it is not necessary to write
     the number.
     When one sodium ion combines with one chloride ion, the formula
     can be written as NaCl, not Na1Cl1.

  5. If more than one polyatomic ion is needed, the ion needs to
     be written in brackets.
     When a hydroxide ion, OH-, combines with an aluminium ion, Al3+,
     the hydroxide ion needs to be written in brackets. The formula for
     aluminium hydroxide is Al(OH)3.

Example 1: Sodium chloride
Write the charge on the sodium and chloride ions.

     Na         Cl

For each sodium ion, how many chloride ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for sodium chloride below.


Example 2: Calcium chloride
Write the charge on the calcium and chloride ions.
      Ca         Cl

For each calcium ion, how many chloride ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for calcium chloride below.
Example 3: Sodium oxide
Write the charge on the sodium and oxide ions.

     Na         O

For each oxide ion, how many sodium ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for sodium oxide below.


Example 4: Magnesium oxide
Write the charge on the magnesium and oxide ions.

     Mg         O

For each magnesium ion, how many oxide ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for magnesium oxide below.


Example 5: Aluminium oxide
Write the charge on the aluminium and oxide ions.

     Al         O

For each aluminium ion, how many oxide ions do you need to balance
the charges? In this situation, you need to find the lowest common
multiple of the charges, in this case 6. How many aluminium ions make
a charge of +6? How many oxide ions make a charge of -6? Write the
formula of aluminium oxide below.


Example 6: Sodium nitrate
Write the charge on the sodium and nitrate ions.

     Na         NO3

For each sodium ion, how may nitrate ions do you need to make the
charges balanced? Write the formula for sodium nitrate below. (Do you
need to use brackets?)


Example 7: Magnesium nitrate
Write the charge on the magnesium and nitrate ions.

     Mg         NO3
 For each magnesium ion, how many nitrate ions do you need to balance

Heat may be taken in or given out during a reaction. Sound, light, movement or
electrical energy may also be produced. When fuels are burnt they give out heat and
light energy. Explosive fuels give out movement and sound energy as well. The
chemical reaction that takes place inside a torch battery gives out electrical energy.

Energy from fuels.

Wood can be burnt asa fuel. Fossil fuels form over millions of years.

Burning of fuels makes carbon dioxide, water and heat energy :
FUEL + OXYGEN i) CARBON DIOXIDE + WATER +

The heat energy can be used to keep our houses warm and to cook food. It can also
be changed into movement energy to drive engines.

Effects on the environment.

Burning fuels release carbon dioxide into the air. This stops heat escaping from the
surface of the Earth back into space. This is called the GREENHOUSE EFFECT and it
may lead to GLOBAL WARMING.

Oil and coal release sulphur dioxide gas when they burn. This gas goes into the air and
dissolves in rain droplets to form ACID RAIN. In some parts of Europe acid rain has
destroyed plant and animal life in lakes and forests. Acid rain also causes corrosion of
buildings and statues.

w.s.38. Solids, liquids and gases. NOte voreeseeseeeseeresisernsee

Everything is made up of particles that are too small to see. The three
states of matter are SOLID, LIQUID and GAS. They all have different
properties due to the arrangement and movement of their particles.

Solids.

The particles are held tightly together by strong
forces. They make small vibrations but they stay
in place. This gives solids a definite shape and
volume. Solids are DENSE (heavy) and they can
not be compressed (squashed) easily because the
particles are already packed closely together.

Liquids.

A liquid can flow because the particles can move
past each other. The particles are still held
closely together by strong forces. Liquids are
DENSE and they can not be compressed easily. A
liquid can change its shape but not its volume.

Gases.

There are only very weak forces between the
particles which are far apart. The particles move
around very quickly and bounce off each other.
Gases have a low density (they are very light)
and they do not have a definite shape or volume.

W.S.50. Types of rock.

Name .....

Rocks can be divided into three main types depending on how they were formed. Read
the information below about the three types of rock.

Igneous rocks.

These are formed when molten magma
cools down and becomes solid. They are
made of tiny crystals, If the magma cools
quickly on the surface of the Earth then
the crystals are small. If the magma cools
slowly, deeper in the Earth's crust, then
the crystals are larger. Igneous rocks are
very hard.

Sedimentary rocks.

These are made from layers of SEDIMENT
(small particles) on the bottom of rivers or
seas. The sediments are compressed as
more layers build up on top of them. The
particles then become cemented together
to form solid rocks, The layers of rock are
called STRATA. Sedimentary rocks have a
grainy structure and they easily crumble.

Metamorphic (changed) rocks.
These are formed from igneous or
sedimentary rocks which are changed
by heat or pressure deep underground.
They are usually harder than the rocks
that formed them.

1. Red-green colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive trait. A woman with normal

2. Haemophilia is a disease caused by a recessive trait on the X chromosome. You are

If you can read this, you are relying on light energy. Light energy and our eyesight are the

Can you imagine what life would be like without light energy? Quite simply, there would
not be any life at all. Plants need light to live and if there were no plants, there would be no
animals, including people.


Sources of Light

Light energy is one of the forms of radiant energy that comes to us from
the Sun. This light energy is formed in nuclear reactions that occur within the Sun.
Other objects and substances can also give off their own light energy. These objects
are said to be luminous. The light carries energy away from luminous objects as
electromagnetic waves.

Absorption and reflection of light

Although sunlight appears to be white, it is not actually a single pure white colour. It is made up of seven different
colours that you can see, called the visible spectrum. The colours of the visible spectrum are red, orange, yellow, green,
indigo and violet. Each of these colours correspond to light of different wavelengths with red light having the longest
wavelength and violet light having the shortest wavelength.

Different materials absorb some of the colours in sunlight (white light) and reflect others. The colour we see in an object
depends on the colours that are reflected back to our eyes. For example, a yellow object absorbs all colours except
yellow, and it reflects yellow.

White objects appear white because they reflect all the colours of sunlight, but black objects appear black because they
absorb all the colours and reflect none.

substance to another, we say that the light is refracted. The light bends when going from one substance to another
because it moves at different speeds through different materials. It travels slower through water and glass than it does
through air.

                                                     9
 We use friction everyday. Sometimes we need friction, and at other times we try to reduce it.
Need friction? We need it for example when:
         we walk. We use the friction between our feet and the
            ground. Imagine trying to walk if there was no friction.
            This would be like walking on ice!
         we drive a car. You could not stop a car without
            friction. You could not start it moving either – the
            wheels would just spin without the car moving. And
            everybody knows what happens if you go too fast
            around a corner or if the road is slippery.
         we use knots or nails. Friction stops knots from coming
            undone, and holds nails in place.
The list goes on and on.

However, friction can also be a hassle. It opposes motion as we have already mentioned. Friction also
produces heat. This can be useful when you rub a match on the side of a box, but it can also cause an engine
to overheat. Friction also causes wear and tear.




    Friction can be a nuisance.
Reducing Friction
There are five different ways of reducing friction.
1. A rolling object meets with less friction than a sliding one. (eg: moving a car on wheels, Egyptions
   moving huge blocks on rolling logs, ball bearings).
2. Lubricants (LOO-bri-cants) such as oil and grease are often used to reduce friction between moving
   parts to reduce wear and tear and make them slide more easily (eg: in machines, on the bearings in
   bicycle and skate board wheels, between bones in our joints).
3. Surfaces in contact can be polished so that they slide over one another more easily. (eg: hulls in racing
   yachts).
4. If air is blown between two surfaces, the friction becomes very small. This is the principle on which a
   hovercraft works.
5. Air resistance is the friction between a moving object and the air it is moving through, and can be
   reduced by giving the object (eg: car, plane) a more streamlined shape. Streamlining is also important
   for objects moving through water (eg: surfboards, speedboats and fast-swimming fish).

                                                     Friction
Have you ever tried to help someone start a car by pushing it? It is very hard to get the car rolling right at the
 start. If you can get the car to move it seems to be easier to push once it has started to move. The car tyres
have a force working against them. This force is trying to stop the car going forward or is said to be resisting
                                   the movement. This force is called friction.

Friction is all around us. It is because of friction that erasers work for us. There is friction




working against us when we ride a bike or skateboard, roller blade, run, play tennis, cut our
food and use a nail file to shape our nails. These are just a few examples of friction at work.
There are several different types of friction:
• Static friction is the force that stops things from starting to move: think of trying to push a car.
•   Sliding friction happens between moving surfaces such as in downhill skiing.
•   Rolling friction happens when a curved surface rolls over another surface. This happens when the wheel
    of a bike turns in one direction and the bike moves in the other direction.
•   Fluid friction happens between fluids or between fluids and solids. Fluid friction is less than friction
    between solids. Fluids are often used to help movement of two solids by reducing the friction between
    the surfaces. The axle on a bike has oil on it to help the metal axle turn more easily inside the casing.

Some sets of scales are marked in newtons but most give a reading in mass units such as kilograms or grams

scales because an object of large mass also has a large weight on Earth.

                                                     Gravity

You can jump in the air but you cannot stay there. You are pulled down by the force of gravity. When you
drop a glass or something falls, it is because gravity pulls the object towards the Earth. This gravitational
force gives objects their weight.

Gravity is the pull of the enormous mass of the Earth on our bodies and any other objects near the Earth’s
surface. It is a non-contact force since it is able to act over a distance, without the objects touching each
other.

There is a small gravitational force that pulls any two objects together. The size of this force depends on:
                the masses of the objects, and
                how far apart they are.

Usually this force is very small, but when one of the objects is the planet Eart, the force is far from small.
This law of gravitation was discovered by Sir Isaac Newton in the seventeenth century.

There is a gravitational pull between the Earth and the moon. This keeps the moon in place and causes tides
on Earth. Similarly, a gravitational pull keeps satellites in orbit around the Earth. The Earth and other planets
are kept in orbit around the sun by a gravitational pull.

We now know that all living things are made up of cells. But the
first time the word cell was used to refer to these tiny units of life

was one of the earliest scientists to study living things under a
microscope. The microscopes of his day were not very strong,

he looked at a thin slice of cork under his microscope, he was
surprised to see what looked like a honeycomb.

Leeuwenhoek (often called the "father of microscopy") in Holland
made other important discoveries using a microscope.

microscopes of his day. In fact, Leeuwenhoek’s microscope was
almost as strong as modern light microscopes. Using his
microscope, Leeuwenhoek discovered tiny animals such as
rotifers. Leeuwenhoek also discovered human blood cells. He

BACKGROUND: A long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away, a great
race of beings lived on a planet called ZORK. The inhabitants were
known as Zorkonians. They are made up of 10 basic genes (unit) that
code for their appearance. Each one of these genes is made up 2
alleles (traits). With this in mind, there are 1,024 different possible
combinations for their appearance! This is called their phenotype or
their physical appearance. If we look at their genes, there are 59,049
different combinations of the alleles! This is called the genotype or
genetic makeup. Remember that we use letters for the alleles that
control the genes and one letter or allele is inherited from each parent.
You will be using Zorks, who use the same genetic principles as a pea
plant, to see how genes are passed on and inherited. You will be using
Punnett Squares to do this.

Here are some things to help you. You must understand these
concepts and terms! I will use traits from the table on the next page
as examples.

Phenotype: The physical appearance or what the gene makes an
organism look like. Examples would be two eyes, yellow hair, and
green lips from a zork.
1. Dominant: The trait that is shown the most. Example: Green hair is
dominant over yellow hair.
2. Recessive: The trait that is hidden. In this example: yellow hair.

Genotype: The genetic makeup of an organism. We use letters for
the genotype. Remember that you need to look at the genotype to see
what the phenotype will be.

Example: There is a Gene or unit for hair color in a zork. The alleles or
traits (individual genes) for hair color would be yellow and green.
There are 2 alleles for each gene and we use letters for each allele.
The capital letters are the dominant alleles and the lower case letters
are the recessive alleles.

                  2. Yellow color = g

1. Heterozygous: The term used for different alleles. There is
always one dominant and one recessive allele. Example: Gg. There is
only one possibility for this!
2. Homozygous: The term used for having the same alleles. This will
be either 2 dominant alleles or 2 recessive alleles. Example: GG or gg.
There are 2 possibilities for this!
